did_you_know.text: The prophecy in this chapter was given in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah—the first year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.
Jeremiah notes that he had been proclaiming the word of the Lord for twenty-three years, since the thirteenth year of Josiah’s reign, but the people had not listened to him.
The Lord repeatedly sent prophets to the people, rising early to speak to them, but the people would not listen.
The prophets’ central message was a call to repentance: to turn from their evil ways and wicked deeds and remain in the land the Lord had given their ancestors.

The destruction is also described as the disappearance of the sounds of everyday life: the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of bridegroom and bride, the sound of millstones, and the light of a lamp.
The land will become desolate, and the nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years.
When the seventy years are completed, the Lord will punish the king of Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans, repaying them for their wrongdoing.
The cup of hot wine symbolizes the prophecy of disaster: Jeremiah is commanded to make the nations to whom the Lord sends him drink from it.
Jerusalem, the cities of Judah, their kings, and their officials are listed first among those who will face judgment; they will be given over to destruction, desolation, and a curse.
The list includes many peoples and kingdoms, and at the end it says that the king of Sheshach will also drink from the cup after them.
